entries.clue: Locked-up prisoner punished for not returning book to library on time? (8)

blocks.note: con is the everyday short word for a convict

blocks.clueFragment: punished for not returning book to library on time
blocks.note: the penalty for an overdue library book is a fine, so the borrower is fined

annotation.surface: A prisoner in his cell, still paying for a library book he kept too long.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Locked-up prisoner' reads as one phrase and is two jobs: the first word defines, the second spells. The question mark concedes that a fine is only one of the punishments on offer.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone confined is shut in and not free to leave, which is what locked-up describes.

entries.clue: Nothing clear somehow? Wise person needed (6)

indicatorNotes.somehow: 'Somehow' admits the letters got there by some route nobody will name, which is licence to take them in any order.

blocks.note: the round letter stands for zero, the crossword's usual nothing
the five letters of CLEAR, re-sorted

annotation.surface: Nothing being clear, and the need for somebody wise to explain it.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the seam where the wordplay stops rather than asking anything. An oracle was the shrine at Delphi whose priestess answered questions, which is why the word still means a source of wisdom.
annotation.definitionFit: An oracle is whoever others go to for authoritative answers, so a wise person is exactly who is wanted.

entries.clue: Female, one with American general – someone hoping to make a catch! (9)

annotation.definition: someone hoping to make a catch

blocks.note: f = female, the form on any official box to tick
the Roman numeral for one
William Tecumseh Sherman, the Union general who marched through Georgia in the American Civil War

annotation.surface: A woman and a companion beside a US general, all of them after a catch.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash is the join: everything before it spells and everything after defines. 'Catch' keeps a second sense alive — the prize a single person lands — which is what the exclamation mark is selling.
annotation.definitionFit: A fisherman sits out with a line waiting for something to take it, so the phrase names him by his whole purpose.

entries.clue: Martial arts exponent contributing to tradition in Japan (5)

indicatorNotes.contributing to: What contributes to something is a part sitting inside it, so the letters are already there in the words that follow.

blocks.note: the letters run on from the tail of 'tradition' through 'in' and into 'Japan', crossing both breaks

annotation.surface: A fighter who is part of the traditional picture of Japan.
annotation.walkthrough: Hidden answers like a clue that says something bland and true, and this one only claims that ninjas are Japanese. The breaks fall mid-word twice, which is what keeps the letters out of sight.
annotation.definitionFit: A ninja was the covert agent of feudal Japan, trained in stealth and in unarmed and armed combat.

entries.clue: Ineffective person gone mad shows resentment (7)

indicatorNotes.mad: Something driven mad no longer behaves in its proper order, and letters out of their proper order have to be rearranged.

blocks.note: a dud is anything that fails to work, the person included
the four letters of GONE, re-sorted

annotation.surface: A useless man who has lost his mind and is plainly aggrieved about something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gone mad' reads as one description of the man and splits into raw material and instruction. Dudgeon has almost vanished from English except in the phrase 'in high dudgeon', which is the sense being defined.
annotation.definitionFit: Dudgeon is a feeling of offence or indignation, the state somebody is in when they go off in high dudgeon.

entries.clue: About to take little medicine with yen to be put right (6)

indicatorNotes.little: A little version of a word is a shortened one, so only the opening syllable of it is wanted.

blocks.note: re = about, the word at the head of a memo
the opening three letters of the word, which is the clipping the clue asks for
the Japanese currency's sign and abbreviation

annotation.surface: Someone about to swallow a small dose and spend some money in the hope of a cure.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Yen' is a longing in the sentence and the Japanese currency in the wordplay, and only the currency pays out a letter. The definition sits at the very end, past two link words that read as ordinary grammar.
annotation.definitionFit: To remedy something is to set right the fault or the illness, so the verbs swap cleanly.

entries.clue: New student joining engineers for training session? (9)

blocks.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineering corps
a fresher is a first-year student at a British university

annotation.surface: A first-year undergraduate signing up with the engineering corps for some training.
annotation.walkthrough: The two pieces arrive in the clue back to front, so the student written first ends up second. The question mark concedes that a refresher is only one sort of training session.
annotation.definitionFit: A refresher is the short course taken to bring knowledge that has lapsed back up to date.

entries.clue: Soldiers on American lists (5)

indicatorNotes.on: In a down entry one thing rests on another by being written above it, so the soldiers take the top of the column.

blocks.note: an officer's men are the soldiers he commands
US is the standard shortening for American

annotation.surface: Troops written up on some American roster.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing in the clue mentions food, and the whole definition is the bare plural 'lists'. A menu is a list of dishes before it is anything else, and a list of options on a screen after that.
annotation.definitionFit: A menu is a list — dishes on a card, choices on a screen — so the plural noun answers 'lists' directly.

entries.clue: Eastern writer in act became more profound (8)

indicatorNotes.in: 'In' is placing rather than joining here: what comes before it is set inside what follows.

blocks.note: a deed is an act, and it splits after two letters to make room
e = eastern, as on a compass
the pen stands for the person who writes with it

annotation.surface: An author from the East appearing in a play, and a thought that grew weightier.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Eastern writer' sounds like one person and is two separate pieces, one of them a single letter. The word holding them is 'act' in its legal-sounding sense, a deed.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that deepened grew greater in depth, and a thought or feeling that gains depth has become more profound.

entries.clue: Fruit and nuts about to be given to boy (6)

indicatorNotes.about: To turn about is to face the other way, so the word before it is read back to front.

blocks.note: nuts means mad, and mad is turned round
a boy in the family is a son

annotation.surface: Fruit and nuts on the point of being handed to a small boy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' looks like the other half of a bowl of fruit and nuts, and it is the slang for mad. A damson is the small dark plum of British hedgerows, grown mostly for jam.
annotation.definitionFit: The damson is a small tart purple plum, so the bare word 'Fruit' names its kind.

entries.clue: Guarded three successive characters, then finished (8)

blocks.note: three letters running consecutively through the alphabet, as the clue asks
a thing that has finished has ended

annotation.surface: Someone who stood up for three people in a row and then was done.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Characters' pulls towards people in a story and wants letters of the alphabet, taken in their running order. Both halves are past tense, which is what keeps the definition honest.
annotation.definitionFit: To defend a place is to guard it against attack, and both words are in the past tense.

entries.clue: Estrange a right troublesome goddess (8)

blocks.note: the letter is the word itself
a lien is a creditor's legal right to hold property until a debt is paid
Ate is the Greek goddess of ruin and reckless folly

annotation.surface: An instruction to fall out with a goddess who is nothing but trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A right' in British speech means 'a thorough' — a right mess, a right nuisance — and that is the reading the sentence wants. The wordplay takes 'right' as the lawyer's kind instead.
annotation.definitionFit: To alienate someone is to turn their affection away until they are a stranger, which is what estrange means.

entries.clue: Son participating in apple festival (6)

indicatorNotes.participating in: Whoever participates in a thing is taking part inside it, so the letter goes within rather than alongside.

blocks.note: British greengrocers divide apples into eaters and cookers, and an eater is the one you bite into raw
s = son, as on a family tree

annotation.surface: A boy taking his part in a festival held for apples.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Apple festival' reads as one event and the two words do entirely separate jobs. The apple wanted is the trade's own word for the eating sort, which crosswords use constantly.
annotation.definitionFit: Easter is the spring feast of the Resurrection, the principal festival of the Christian year.

entries.clue: Awful pains – mothers who hate people? (12)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a relative clause with its subject left implied — 'those who hate people' — which is a standard way of defining a plural noun for a kind of person.

indicatorNotes.Awful: What is awful is in a bad state, and letters in a bad state are not sitting in the order they were handed over.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters across the two words

annotation.surface: Terrible aches, and the mothers who cannot stand anybody.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash reads as a pause in a list and does no work at all — both words are raw material. The answer comes from the Greek misein, to hate, and anthropos, man.
annotation.definitionFit: Misanthropes despise humanity in general, so the clause names them by the single trait that defines them.

entries.clue: Eccentric priest, man bringing a particular flavour (9)

indicatorNotes.Eccentric: An eccentric thing is off its proper centre, and letters knocked off their proper places need putting somewhere new.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters across the two words

annotation.surface: An odd clergyman and his companion arriving with a taste all of their own.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flavour' in the sentence is the figurative kind a character brings to a room, and the answer needs the literal one off a packet. Spearmint is the garden mint whose pointed leaves gave it the name.
annotation.definitionFit: Spearmint is the mint used in chewing gum and toothpaste, so it names one flavour rather than a class of them.

entries.clue: How tree is dealt with differently (9)

indicatorNotes.dealt with: To be dealt with is to be handled, and letters that have been handled no longer lie where they were found.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters across the three words

annotation.surface: A question about a tree that is being handled in some unusual way.
annotation.walkthrough: The missing article is the tell: 'How tree is' will not parse as English, and a phrase that will not parse is usually a bag of letters waiting to be tipped out.
annotation.definitionFit: Otherwise means in another way, so it stands in for 'differently' wherever the adverb is wanted.

entries.clue: Bully, horrible to maiden (8)

indicatorNotes.horrible: Something horrible has been made a mess of, and a mess of letters is simply a new order for them.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters across the two words

annotation.surface: A bully being vile to a young woman.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma is the seam, and everything past it is letters — the sentence reads as a complete accusation, which is why the join hides. A maiden is often the M of cricket's scoreless over, but here she is only the girl.
annotation.definitionFit: To dominate someone is to hold power over them and push them about, which is what a bully does.

entries.clue: Part of military parade finds nobleman with hesitation at start of month (12)

indicatorNotes.at start of: To be put at the start of a word is to go in front of it, which fixes where the pieces already spelt out land.

blocks.note: a count is the continental nobleman ranking with an English earl
er is the noise made while hesitating
the third month of the year

annotation.surface: A nobleman hesitating at the beginning of the month while a parade goes past.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue pays for March the month and gets March the step thrown in, which is why the surface sits so comfortably in a parade. ER is the crossword's standard noise of hesitation.
annotation.definitionFit: A countermarch is the drill movement in which a column turns and marches back down its own line, one of the figures a parade is built from.

entries.clue: Yours truly atop a home most miserly (7)

indicatorNotes.atop: In a down entry whatever sits atop something else is written above it, so that piece takes the top of the column.

blocks.note: the letter-writer's way of saying me
the letter is the word itself
a nest is the bird's home

annotation.surface: The writer perched on the roof of somebody's house, in a thoroughly tight-fisted mood.
annotation.walkthrough: The home is the bird's, not the householder's, and nothing in the sentence hints at it. 'Yours truly' closes a letter and crosswords take it for those two letters every time.
annotation.definitionFit: The meanest of a group is the one least willing to part with money, which is what most miserly says.

entries.clue: Lectures without passion aboard ship (6)

indicatorNotes.aboard: Whatever goes aboard a vessel is carried inside it, so those letters are shut in rather than added on.

blocks.note: SS heads a ship's name for steamship, and splits to let the cargo in
somebody with no passion in them is cold

annotation.surface: Dry, passionless talks delivered to passengers on board a ship.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole sentence is one idea — dull lectures at sea — and the definition is only its first word. 'Lectures' is the telling-off sense, the one a parent gives, not the one a professor does.
annotation.definitionFit: To scold is to tell somebody off at length, and 'lectures' carries that same sense of a dressing-down.

entries.clue: Very cold beer (6)

blocks.note: the piercing kind of cold a British forecast warns about in a hard frost, said of a wind
the hoppy brown ale ordered by the pint in any British pub

annotation.surface: An ice-cold pint.
annotation.walkthrough: Two words and two separate definitions, joined by nothing, which is why they read as one ordinary phrase. Bitter is served at cellar temperature and never chilled, so the picture the clue paints could not happen.
annotation.definitionFit: Bitter describes a piercing cold, as in a bitter wind, and is also the name of Britain's everyday hoppy ale.

entries.clue: Guy drinks last of wine (5)

indicatorNotes.last of: The last of a word is the letter it finishes on, so only that closing letter is taken.

blocks.note: teas are drinks, the plural of the national cup
the letter the word ends on

annotation.surface: A man at the table working his way down to the last of the wine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Guy' is a verb here, and the sentence does everything it can to keep it a noun. Guy Fawkes is behind the word: his effigy was carried round and jeered at, which is how guying came to mean mocking.
annotation.definitionFit: To guy somebody is to hold them up to ridicule, the same mockery that tease covers.

entries.clue: Sailor’s pamphlet gives summary (8)

blocks.note: AB is an able seaman, and the apostrophe-s of the possessive comes along with him
a tract is a short pamphlet, usually pressing a religious or political case

annotation.surface: A leaflet belonging to a sailor.
annotation.walkthrough: The possessive is not possessive: the apostrophe-s hands over a letter rather than an owner, which is easy to read straight past. An abstract is the paragraph of summary printed at the head of a scientific paper.
annotation.definitionFit: An abstract is the condensed statement of what a longer piece of writing says, which is a summary.

entries.clue: A pie’s cooked – it’s a shade of brown (5)

indicatorNotes.cooked: What goes into the pot comes out changed beyond recognition, so the letters arrive in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 5 letters counting the apostrophe-s

annotation.surface: A pie out of the oven and browned on top.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is fodder rather than possession: it stands for 'is' in the sentence and for a letter in the wordplay. Sepia is the brown ink of the cuttlefish, which is how old photographs of that colour got the name.
annotation.definitionFit: Sepia is the dark reddish brown of cuttlefish ink and of faded photographs, so it names one shade of brown.

entries.clue: Military depot in periodical publication (8)

blocks.note: the building or shipboard compartment where ammunition and explosives are stored
the weekly or monthly of articles and pictures carries the same name

annotation.surface: An arms store written up in this month's issue of something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' joins and does nothing else, which is what lets two definitions pass for one sentence. The store came first: the word arrives from Arabic makhzan, a warehouse, and the periodical is a warehouse of articles.
annotation.definitionFit: A magazine is the store where ammunition is kept, and equally the illustrated periodical on the newsstand.

entries.clue: Documentation reportedly in small bottles! (6)

indicatorNotes.reportedly: What is reported is passed on by mouth, so the word is wanted for the sound it makes rather than the way it is spelt.

blocks.note: documentation is kept in files, and PH says F, so the two words come out of the mouth identically

annotation.surface: Paperwork that is apparently being stored in little glass bottles.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark flags the absurdity — nobody files anything in a bottle — and that is the only hint that the first word is there to be said aloud. A phial is the stoppered glass tube a chemist's sample comes in.
annotation.definitionFit: Phials are the little stoppered glass containers used for medicines and samples, so 'small bottles' names them plainly.

entries.clue: Material bringing this writer into a bit of money (6)

indicatorNotes.into: Going into something means landing inside it, so those letters are planted within rather than set beside.

blocks.note: a cent is the smallest coin of the dollar and of the euro
the setter pointing at himself

annotation.surface: Something an author has written that is earning him a modest sum.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Material' reads as the stuff a writer works up into a book, and the answer is the builder's kind entirely. Crosswords take 'this writer' for ME whenever the setter points at himself.
annotation.definitionFit: Cement is the powdered binder that sets hard with water, one of the basic building materials.

entries.clue: Translated a bit of poetry, making one cross (8)

blocks.note: tr. is the abbreviation printed on a title page when a book has been translated
the letter is the word itself
a verse is one stanza, a bit of a poem

annotation.surface: A translator has had a go at a short poem and annoyed somebody in the process.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Making one cross' promises irritation and delivers a verb of movement instead, which is the whole difficulty of the last three words. A verse is a portion of a poem, never the poem itself.
annotation.definitionFit: To traverse a stretch of country is to go across it from one side to the other, so the verbs swap directly.
